1.pericope_label: Then they told David, saying, Behold, the Philistines fight against Keilah, and they rob the threshingfloors. Therefore David enquired of the Lord, saying, Shall I go and smite these Philistines? And the Lord said unto David, Go, and smite the Philistines, and save Keilah. And David’s men said unto him, Behold, we be afraid here in Judah: how much more then if we come to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines? Then David enquired of the Lord yet again. And the Lord answered him and said, Arise, go down to Keilah; for I will deliver the Philistines into thine hand. So David and his men went to Keilah, and fought with the Philistines, and brought away their cattle, and smote them with a great slaughter. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah. And it came to pass, when Abiathar the son of Ahimelech fled to David to Keilah, that he came down with an ephod in his hand.

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the mode of enquiry the chapter's first problem. It cannot have been through the ephod, he argues, since the narrative itself says Abiathar only joined David at Keilah, after the citizens had asked for aid; so the enquiry was made through Gad the prophet, who was with David, and he supports this from the parallel of Jehoshaphat enquiring of Micaiah, where the same formula is used. He then diagnoses the whole difficulty: the versions and the commentators failed to understand that enquiry of the Lord could be made in any other mode than through the Urim, and he holds that the Greek translators must have deliberately altered the Hebrew to escape it. He also sets the episode in the decline of Saul, whose malady concentrated his whole thought on David's imaginary crimes until the history of the latter part of his reign is little more than a recital of bewildered efforts to compass the young hero's destruction, and clears up the geography, that the men of Keilah saying they were afraid here in Judah does not put their town outside the tribe but only shows the district round it under Philistine domination. Delitzsch gives the chapter its theological frame, that the Lord gave his servant pledges of the kingdom while plunging him into deeper and deeper trouble, to refine him and train him to be a king after his own heart.

Gill leaves the mechanism of the enquiry alone and takes up instead why David hesitated, that he had no commission from his prince to act and that his force was so small that attacking the Philistine army might be hazardous. The prudential reading makes the men's reluctance, and David's repeated enquiry, a matter of ordinary military judgment rather than of weak faith.

Clarke takes the opposite road on the enquiry and does to the order of the text what Ellicott accuses the Greek of doing to its sense: the enquiry was probably by means of Abiathar, and therefore he thinks, with Houbigant, that the sixth verse should be read immediately after the first. On David's motive he names the alternative that was open, that the adventure was truly noble, since had David not loved his country above private revenge he would have rejoiced in this invasion, and in most cases a man with David's wrongs would have joined with his country's enemies.

Henry reads the prophet's earlier order as a commission: since Saul neglected the public safety, David was to take care of it notwithstanding the ill treatment given him, rendering good for evil and so being a type of him who not only ventured his life but laid it down for those who were his enemies. He suggests a cause for the raid, that the departure of both God and David from Saul probably encouraged the Philistines, and draws the rule that the way for any country to be quiet is to let God's church be quiet in it. He admires the public spirit of a man whose own hands were full and whose life Saul sought, yet who was willing to serve Saul's interests against the common enemy and bravely abhorred the thought of sacrificing the common welfare to his private revenge.

debates: How David enquired of the Lord before Abiathar is said to have arrived, where Ellicott argues it must have been through Gad the prophet and that the Greek translators altered the Hebrew to hide the difficulty, while Clarke holds it was by means of Abiathar and moves the sixth verse up after the first on Houbigant's proposal.

Why David hesitated before going, where Gill gives prudential reasons, that he had no commission from his prince and that his force was small, while Henry treats the going as a duty already laid on him by the prophet's commission.

What the men of Keilah meant by saying they were afraid here in Judah, which Ellicott takes not as placing the town outside the tribe but as showing the surrounding district under Philistine domination.
outliers: Delitzsch frames the whole chapter as the Lord giving David pledges of the kingdom while plunging him into deeper trouble, to refine him and train him to be a king after his own heart.
Clarke observes that in most cases a man with David's wrongs would have joined with his country's enemies, which is what makes the relief of Keilah noble rather than merely dutiful.

7.pericope_label: And it was told Saul that David was come to Keilah. And Saul said, God hath delivered him into mine hand; for he is shut in, by entering into a town that hath gates and bars. And Saul called all the people together to war, to go down to Keilah, to besiege David and his men. And David knew that Saul secretly practised mischief against him; and he said to Abiathar the priest, Bring hither the ephod. Then said David, O Lord God of Israel, thy servant hath certainly heard that Saul seeketh to come to Keilah, to destroy the city for my sake. Will the men of Keilah deliver me up into his hand? will Saul come down, as thy servant hath heard? O Lord God of Israel, I beseech thee, tell thy servant. And the Lord said, He will come down. Then said David, Will the men of Keilah deliver me and my men into the hand of Saul? And the Lord said, They will deliver thee up. Then David and his men, which were about six hundred, arose and departed out of Keilah, and went whithersoever they could go. And it was told Saul that David was escaped from Keilah; and he forbare to go forth.

schools.summary: Ellicott credits Saul with a tactician's calculation: there was little chance of taking a man roaming at large through the desert, but real hope of compassing his destruction by treachery or hand-to-hand encounter in a confined space like a city with bars and gates, and Saul and his counsellors knew too well what to expect of that faithless, thankless city. He finds the impiety written into the vocabulary, the Hebrew word saying that God has repudiated or rejected him where the Greek translators render it sold him, and notes that the summons to war was always a royal right. On the enquiry he observes that a different method is plainly in use here, the narrative first recording that Abiathar had arrived with the ephod and then having David direct him to bring it; in that ephod were twelve precious stones, one for each tribe with the tribal names engraved, which by ancient tradition only the high priest might use as oracles. On the inverted questions he reports Dean Payne Smith's view that they were put according to their relative importance in David's mind and then answered in logical order, and cites the Talmud rule that the enquirer is not to ask about two things at a time. Delitzsch draws the same rule from the text, that the enquirer laid his matter before God in prayer and received an answer, but always to one question only, so David had to ask his first again.

Gill supplies the ingratitude plainly, that Saul must have been told why David went to Keilah, which one would have thought would have reconciled his mind to him, whereas it only led him to contrive mischief. He notes that the summons was proclaimed by a herald through all parts of the kingdom, the prerogative of a king, and that the questions are not orderly put, the last standing where the first should be, which shows the perturbation of mind David was in on hearing Saul's design.

Clarke reads the scene more simply, as though David himself, clothed with the ephod, consulted the Lord, and then finds in the two answers an ample proof that there is such a thing as contingency in human affairs, God having poised many things between a possibility of being and not being. The answers carried conditions, that if David stayed Saul would come down and that if Saul came down the men of Keilah would betray him, and because David left, neither happened; so a positive declaration of God about something in which man is to be employed does not destroy free agency. Wesley settles the manner of the answer, that it came not by any change in the colour or situation of the stones in the breastplate but by a voice or suggestion from God to the high priest, and agrees that the answer, like the question, was upon supposition.

Henry presses past Saul's ingratitude to his impiety: in saying God hath delivered him into my hand, Saul made providence patronise his malicious design, and he triumphed before the victory, forgetting how often he had held fairer advantages against David and missed his aim; one smiling providence, Henry warns, neither justifies an unrighteous cause nor secures its success. The summons abused the Israel of God as well, the people marched out under pretence of opposing the Philistines, for miserable is that people whose prince is a tyrant, since some are sufferers by his tyranny and others are made instruments of it. Where Saul complains that David deals very subtilely, Henry answers that all David's subtlety was to secure himself. He turns the ephod to use, that no sooner is it brought than David employs it, and we who have the scriptures in our hands should take advice from them in doubtful cases and learn to say, Bring hither the Bible, admiring also a prayer that was more solicitous for the city than for himself.

debates: How the answer came through the ephod, where Wesley holds it was by a voice or suggestion from God to the high priest rather than by any change in the stones, Ellicott describes the twelve engraved gems as themselves permitted to serve as oracles, and Clarke reads the scene as though David himself wore the ephod.

Why David's two questions stand in the wrong order, where Gill takes the inversion as a symptom of his perturbation of mind, Ellicott reports the view that it followed their relative importance in his mind, and Delitzsch derives from it the rule that only one question is answered at a time.

Whether the divine answers were unconditional, where Clarke and Wesley both read them as given upon supposition, so that Saul's not coming and David's not being betrayed prove contingency rather than a failed prediction.
outliers: Ellicott notes that the Hebrew word Saul uses says God has repudiated or rejected David, where the Greek translators render it sold him.
Clarke finds in this short history an ample proof of contingency in human affairs, God having poised many things between a possibility of being and not being.

14.pericope_label: And David abode in the wilderness in strong holds, and remained in a mountain in the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul sought him every day, but God delivered him not into his hand. And David saw that Saul was come out to seek his life: and David was in the wilderness of Ziph in a wood. And Jonathan Saul’s son arose, and went to David into the wood, and strengthened his hand in God. And he said unto him, Fear not: for the hand of Saul my father shall not find thee; and thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee; and that also Saul my father knoweth. And they two made a covenant before the Lord: and David abode in the wood, and Jonathan went to his house.

schools.summary: Delitzsch fixes the ground: the desert of Judah is the tract between the mountains of Judah and the Dead Sea, and the desert of Ziph the part surrounding that town, whose name survives in the ruins of Tell Zif; the wood is probably a proper name for a district there overgrown with bushes. Ellicott puts the wilderness between Hebron and En-gedi while admitting that some stations in the future king's wanderings are only doubtfully identified, and notes that some read the wood as the proper name Horesh. He reads the remark that Saul sought him every day but God delivered him not into his hand as a general notice covering the remaining portion of the reign, and hears a quiet irony in it, that armed with all the power of the king in Israel Saul was powerless because the invisible King of Israel declined to give this hated David into his hand. He rejects as untenable the idea that this last interview between the friends was transposed here from the earlier secret meeting, since the narrative is circumstantial and names the scene, and takes the phrase that Jonathan strengthened his hand in God as the narrator's own signal of how sorely tried David was, pressed by the relentless hostility of his sovereign, the apparent hopelessness of the struggle and the ingratitude of whole bodies of his countrymen. Delitzsch adds that the covenant made here was a renewal of the earlier one by another solemn oath.

Gill measures the friendship by the journey, some twenty-two miles from Gibeah to the place where David was. He also asks how David knew Saul had come out against him, and offers either that he saw him with his bodily eyes from the top of the mountain or that he was informed by his friends, perhaps by Jonathan himself or by spies sent to observe Saul's motions, and notes that the covenant was renewed in the name and fear of God and before him as a witness.

Clarke thinks there was always a secret intercourse between David and Jonathan, by which David was kept informed of his father's designs, and insists that Jonathan could do all of this consistently with his duty to his father and his king, since he knew God had appointed David to the kingdom and came to encourage him to trust the Most High. Wesley describes the strengthening as comfort and support against all his fears, by minding him of God's infallible promises and of the singular providence which hitherto had been and still would be with him, and reads the words I shall be next unto thee as a plain renunciation: Jonathan does not look to be king himself, as by his birth he might expect, but takes a secondary place inferior to David. He adds the sad note that they parted here and never came together again that we find in this world.

Henry asks us first to commend David's conduct in these hiding places, his humility, fidelity to his prince and patient attendance on the providence of his God, since he did not draw up his forces against Saul to avenge his own quarrel and that of the murdered priests, though that would have ended his troubles and the country's calamities, but kept God's way and waited God's time, content to secure himself in woods and wildernesses even though to some this might seem a reproach to the courage for which he had been famous. Then he asks us to lament the fate, that an innocent man should be put in fear of his life and a man of merit so recompensed. Saul seeking him every day shows how restless his malice was, and seeking his life how cruel. On Jonathan he distinguishes three offices: the pious friend, who strengthened his hand not in the creature but in God by reminding him of the promise and the holy oil; the self-denying friend, who counted it preferment enough to be next him though under him; and the constant friend, who renewed the league a third time before the Lord.

debates: What Jonathan's strengthening of David's hand in God consisted of, where Henry and Wesley fill it with the promise, the anointing oil and the providence that had been with him hitherto, while Ellicott reads the phrase as the narrator's comment on how near despair David had come.

How the words I shall be next unto thee should be taken, where Wesley makes them a renunciation of a birthright Jonathan might have expected, Henry calls it self-denying friendship that cleared David's way, and Ellicott treats it as a pledge never put to the test because of Gilboa.

Whether this interview belongs here at all, which Ellicott defends against the suggestion of transposition from the earlier secret meeting, on the ground that the narrative is circumstantial and even names the scene.
outliers: Ellicott hears a quiet irony in the general notice that Saul sought David every day, since armed with all the power of the king in Israel he was powerless, the invisible King of Israel declining to give David into his hand.
Wesley notes that the two friends parted here and never came together again that we find in this world.

19.pericope_label: Then came up the Ziphites to Saul to Gibeah, saying, Doth not David hide himself with us in strong holds in the wood, in the hill of Hachilah, which is on the south of Jeshimon? Now therefore, O king, come down according to all the desire of thy soul to come down; and our part shall be to deliver him into the king’s hand. And Saul said, Blessed be ye of the Lord; for ye have compassion on me. Go, I pray you, prepare yet, and know and see his place where his haunt is, and who hath seen him there: for it is told me that he dealeth very subtilly. See therefore, and take knowledge of all the lurking places where he hideth himself, and come ye again to me with the certainty, and I will go with you: and it shall come to pass, if he be in the land, that I will search him out throughout all the thousands of Judah. And they arose, and went to Ziph before Saul: but David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the plain on the south of Jeshimon. Saul also and his men went to seek him. And they told David: wherefore he came down into a rock, and abode in the wilderness of Maon. And when Saul heard that, he pursued after David in the wilderness of Maon. And Saul went on this side of the mountain, and David and his men on that side of the mountain: and David made haste to get away for fear of Saul; for Saul and his men compassed David and his men round about to take them. But there came a messenger unto Saul, saying, Haste thee, and come; for the Philistines have invaded the land. Wherefore Saul returned from pursuing after David, and went against the Philistines: therefore they called that place Sela–hammahlekoth. And David went up from thence, and dwelt in strong holds at En–gedi.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the words of the Ziphites and the king's reply as proof that they were warm adherents of Saul, entirely devoted to his fortunes and well aware of his desire to be rid of David. He settles the geography, that Jeshimon is not a place but a word for desert or solitude, used here of the dreary tract between the Dead Sea and the Hebron mountains, the wilderness of Judea the Gospel speaks of; that the thousands of Judah were the greater tribal divisions, Judah being named as David's own tribe where Saul probably found the larger number of his adherents; and that the name of Maon is preserved in a village built on a prominent conical hill. He quotes a modern commentator calling the Philistine invasion God's plan to save David, the Philistines having probably availed themselves of the withdrawal of Saul's forces southward. Delitzsch traces Saul's blessing of the traitors to an evil conscience, that suspecting David of seeking to become his murderer he thanked God in his delusion that the Ziphites had compassion on him, and sets out the charge laid on them, to reconnoitre the place where David's foot came and find who had seen him there, lest false reports deceive him, and then to come again with the certainty. He places Maon less than four hours south of Hebron and two from Ziph, and prefers the rock of smoothnesses, that is of slipping away, to the rock of divisions.

Gill supplies the motive the narrative withholds, that the Ziphites, though of David's own tribe, were terrified by what Saul had done to Nob and judged it safest for their own security to inform against him; and he places Saul at Gibeah, where he kept his court, returned from an earlier search. On the messenger he reports that he came from the court by order of the council there, adding that the Jews say it was an angel from heaven, but that whichever it was it was certainly the providence of God directing the affair, that a messenger should come just at the moment when David was likely to fall into Saul's hands. He closes with the narrowness of the escape.

Clarke takes the messenger as providence exerted for the salvation of David's life: God had already prepared the invasion of the land by the Philistines and kept Saul ignorant how far David was in his power, and the message arrived just at the point of time, since the advanced guards and scouts must have discovered him in a very short time. On the place-name he keeps the rock of divisions, giving the Targum's reason, that the heart of the king was divided to go hither and thither, and that here Saul was obliged to separate himself from David in order to oppose the invaders. Wesley observes that the Ziphites were of David's own tribe, for which unnatural carriage he calls them strangers in the Psalm, that the rock David came down to was a cave in the rock, and that the wisdom of God is never at a loss for ways and means to preserve his people.

Henry weighs the treachery by what the Ziphites owed David: he had put the more confidence in the people of that country because they were of his own tribe, and they had reason to think themselves happy in serving the ornament of their tribe, a man so far from plundering their country that he was ready to protect it; yet they told Saul exactly where David quartered and invited him down, unasked and without even requesting a reward, as Judas did. In Saul's blessing of them he hears how near God was to his mouth though far from his heart, and in his complaint that they had compassion on him a self-pity that his own envy and ill-nature had earned him. He assigns the fifty-fourth Psalm to this hour and draws the chase as the narrative gives it, Saul so close that there was but a mountain between, David in fear and Saul in hope, the mountain itself an emblem of divine providence coming between David and the destroyer, like the pillar of cloud between Israel and the Egyptians. He suspects Saul would not have broken off the pursuit had no private interest of his own been at stake.

debates: What the place-name means, where Delitzsch prefers the rock of smoothnesses, that is of slipping away or escaping, as the better supported derivation, while Clarke keeps the rock of divisions and gives the Targum's reason that the king's heart was divided to go hither and thither.

Who sent the messenger that saved David, where Gill reports that he came from the court by order of the council, notes the Jewish tradition of an angel from heaven, and insists either way on the providence of God, while Clarke holds that God had already prepared the invasion itself.

Why Saul broke off a pursuit he had nearly won, where Henry suspects a private interest of his own in the invaded territory, since he had cared so little for Keilah's distress, while Ellicott quotes a modern commentator calling the invasion simply God's plan to save David.
outliers: Henry notes that the Ziphites betrayed David unasked and without even requesting a reward, unlike Judas, who at least asked what he would be given.
Gill supplies the motive the narrative withholds, that the Ziphites were terrified by what Saul had done to Nob and informed against David for their own security.
